title: Comments of Chevron U.S.A., Inc. on the proposed Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking re the Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System under RM26-4.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Interconnection of Large Loads                          )              Docket No.          RM26-4-000
to the Interstate Transmission System                   )


                             COMMENTS OF CHEVRON U.S.A., INC.

        In accordance with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) October

27, 2025, Notice Inviting Comments and its November 7, Notice of Extension of Time, Chevron

U.S.A., Inc. (Chevron) respectfully submits its initial comments in this proceeding. Chevron

emphatically agrees with the Secretary of Energy that the timely and orderly interconnection of

large loads constitutes an “urgent issue that requires prompt attention.”1 Chevron encourages the

Commission to seize this opportunity to facilitate the expedited interconnection of large loads and

generation to support it, including co-located generation. In doing so, the Commission should take

a practical approach that avoids disputes over jurisdictional issues or regional variations and that

provides regulatory certainty as soon as practicable to support major near-term generation

investment decisions.

        Chevron is one of the world’s leading integrated energy companies. We believe affordable,

reliable and ever cleaner energy is essential to enabling human progress. Chevron is both a large

energy user and an energy supplier, with plans to deliver scalable, reliable natural gas-fired projects

to serve co-located data centers in the U.S. that will lead speed to market and may have the

I.      BACKGROUND

        On October 23, 2025, the Secretary of Energy, pursuant to his authority under section 403

of the Department of Energy Organization Act (DOE Act), directed the Commission to initiate

rulemaking procedures and consider an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking (ANOPR) to

standardize and accelerate “large load” interconnections to the interstate transmission system.2 The

DOE ANOPR is an appropriate response to the extraordinary growth in U.S. electricity demand

“due, in large part to the rapid growth of large loads.”3 It is also consistent with the President’s

declaration that the United States is facing a national energy emergency and his prioritization of

the development of artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and new, reliable generation as major

components of America’s economic and national security.4

        Chevron previously urged the Commission in the PJM co-location proceeding to act boldly

to eliminate regulatory obstacles and to provide regulatory certainty that would facilitate the kinds

of major investments that Chevron is considering.5 The DOE ANOPR presents a new opportunity

to do so, and the Commission should move quickly to take advantage of it. Simply stated, Chevron

wants to invest billions of dollars to build the power generation needed to enable America’s AI

II.     COMMENTS

        A.       The Commission Should Seize the Opportunity to Provide Clear Regulatory
                 Guidance to Expedite Large Load Interconnections Including Related Co-
                 Location Arrangements

        The U.S. power grid is at an inflection point: load is growing at an unprecedented rate 7—

driven by data centers,8 growing industrial demands, and increased electrification—as power plant

retirements are peaking.9 The rapid growth of power demand requires cost-effective, reliable and

scalable solutions to enable growth and avoid burdening the existing grid – and the speed and scale

of the solutions matters in meeting this power demand growth. Chevron believes that solutions

like natural gas-fired power can provide the reliable, lower carbon intensity power needed to fuel

American AI innovation.

        The DOE ANOPR offers the Commission a roadmap for facilitating the expeditious

interconnection of large loads and supporting generation to the interstate transmission system in a

way that is wholly consistent with the President’s priorities. Ensuring the timely and orderly

 interconnection of large loads, including data centers, is vital for the Nation’s economic and

national security; the Commission should seize this opportunity with dispatch.

         Specifically, the Commission should move forward with a rulemaking that generally

accords with, and further develops, the fourteen principles set forth in the DOE ANOPR. After

considering comments on the DOE ANOPR, the Commission should promptly issue a Notice of

Proposed Rulemaking (NOPR) that fleshes out DOE’s initial recommendations and includes

specific regulatory text. The Commission should set an expedited timetable for NOPR comments

and do everything practicable to meet the Secretary’s April 30, 2026, deadline for final action.

         In addition, Chevron previously urged the Commission to “take creative and aggressive

action to allow new generation resources to quickly reach commercial operations and provide

essential reliability services to the grid in addition to energy to the data centers themselves” and

“to encourage the development of co-location arrangements.”10 The DOE ANOPR also expresses

support for co-location, which it refers to as “hybrid” arrangements.11 The Commission should

ensure that the steps it takes in this proceeding prioritize the development of hybrid arrangements

that involve major investments in new generation resources to achieve the maximum electric

supply buildout necessary for domestic data centers as soon as practicable.

         B.         The Commission Should Support Interim Regional Fast Track
                    Interconnection Processes for Large Loads and Co-Located Generation to
                    Support Them

          In its Co-Location Comments, Chevron urged the Commission to create a separate,

expedited co-located load and generation interconnection process. 12 Since April, the Commission

accepted temporary “fast-track” proposals—the Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS)

processes—in both the Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) and Midcontinent Independent System

Operator, Inc. (MISO).13 The ERAS orders recognize that urgent near-term resource adequacy and

reliability concerns due to load growth, generation retirement, and delays in the interconnection

process can warrant expedited interconnection procedures. ERAS provides for an accelerated

study of certain interconnection requests to ensure near-term resource adequacy and/or reliability

needs. 14 These types of proposals could be models for new fast-track mechanisms to quickly

interconnect large loads and related generation. New power generation projects for data centers

should not wait years in interconnection queues to reach commercial operations.

         Fast-tracking mechanisms are consistent with the DOE ANOPR’s overarching goals as

well as DOE’s stated openness to new proposals under section 205 of the Federal Power Act and

to hybrid co-location arrangements. 15 SPP recently proposed a High Impact Large Load

Generation Assessment (HILLGA) process includes a mechanism for paired large loads and

        C.         The Commission Should Allow for Regional Flexibility While Still Requiring
                   Speedy Action

        The DOE ANOPR contemplates establishing national large load interconnection standards

similar to the generator interconnection standards established under Order Nos. 2003, 845, and

2023.17 uut the Commission’s generation interconnection rules are not identical in all regions.

Rather, the Commission has allowed the Independent System Operator/Regional Transmission

Organizations (ISO/RTO) regions to adopt “independent entity variations” that better suit region-

specific circumstances where the ISO/RTO demonstrates that the proposed variation: (1) is just

and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential; and (2) accomplishes the purposes

of the Commission’s generator interconnection requirements.18

        The Commission should take a similar approach with respect to large load

interconnections. As the Commission has previously recognized, each ISO/RTO “has different

operating characteristics depending on its size and location” and, therefore, should “have

Allowing for appropriate flexibility should facilitate the adoption of large load interconnection

standards by ensuring that such standards can be efficiently and expediently implemented

according to each region’s needs. Preserving flexibility is also consistent with the DOE ANOPR’s

statement that it “is not intended in any way to discourage public utilities from making filings to

address these and similar issues under [Federal Power Act (FPA)] section 205.”20

         D.         The Commission Should Seek to Minimize Jurisdictional Conflicts in Order to
                    Facilitate the Timely Adoption of Large Load Interconnection Standards

         The FPA authorizes the Commission to regulate “the sale of electric energy at wholesale in

interstate commerce,” including both wholesale electricity rates and any rule or practice directly

“affecting” such rates.21 “The law places beyond the [Commission’s] power, and leaves to the

States alone, the regulation of ‘any other sale’—most notably, any retail sale—of electricity.”22

         The DOE ANOPR appears to be intended to stay within the bounds of the Commission’s

jurisdiction over interconnections to interstate transmission facilities.23 Chevron believes that this

is a sound approach and recommends that the Commission focus on developing large load

would maximize near-term benefits to avoid jurisdictional disputes that would threaten to delay

the implementation, and the legal durability, of the Commission’s directives in this proceeding.

        Chevron is mindful that state regulators have raised jurisdictional concerns about the DOE

ANOPR.24 Chevron takes no position on the potential merits of such concerns at this time but

reserves the right to respond in future submissions. States should take comfort from the

Commission’s recent order in Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc., which

rejected a proposed “High Impact Load Tariff” on the basis that it impermissibly dictated “the

terms and conditions of a [customer’s] retail service in ways that are beyond the Commission’s

authority.” 25 And the Commission should seek to resolve legitimate state concerns while still

taking decisive action within its purview to accelerate large load interconnections.

        In that vein, the Commission should seek to coordinate with states on large load

interconnection matters, e.g., through the ongoing Federal-State Current Issues Collaborative.26

Chevron has direct experience with the benefits of federal-state cooperation. For example,

Chevron owns approximately 1.1 gigawatts of cogeneration in California, connected both in front

of the meter and behind the meter, that currently provide essential services to the grid, such as

resource adequacy, emergency energy, and ancillary services. The development of these

cogeneration assets was facilitated, in part, by the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978

implementation and enforcement of PURPA’s requirements. PURPA thereby allowed for flexibility

in adapting federal standards to local circumstances and needs. The Commission should be open

to similar approaches as it works on standards to facilitate the interconnection of large loads. This

could include making use of the federal-state joint board mechanism under section 209 of the FPA.

         E.         The Commission Should Consider Invoking its Reliability Jurisdiction Under
                    Section 215 of the FPA

         In its Co-Location Comments, Chevron recommended that the Commission invoke its

authority under section 215 of the FPA to “create a separate co-located load interconnection

process to expeditiously study and manage the coordinated interconnection of large loads co-

located with generation facilities.”27 Although the DOE ANOPR does not reference section 215,

the Commission should use its authority under that provision to the full extent that it deems

necessary to address large load interconnections. The North American Electric Reliability

Corporation has acknowledged the potentially substantial reliability impact of large loads. It

recently submitted a report to the Commission explaining how it aims to address the impacts of,

and integrate, large loads in reliability planning requirements.28 The breadth of the Commission’s

jurisdiction under section 215 could be used to reinforce the legal basis of actions that the

Commission may take in this proceeding.29

 III.   CONCLUSION

       The Secretary of Energy has presented the Commission with an unprecedented opportunity

to facilitate the speedy interconnection of large loads and supporting co-located generation. The

Commission should act quickly, while avoiding distracting jurisdictional disputes with states and

accommodating constructive regional proposals. Taking that approach will be most likely to

provide regulatory certainty and to encourage large load and electric infrastructure investments

that will maximize economic and national security benefits as rapidly as practicable.
